extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the MPEP Alice/Mayo framework to determine whether a patent claim: (1) recites a statutory category and (2) is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon), including the two-prong Step 2A inquiry and related examiner best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1: Whether a claim is to a statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 asks: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter? Evaluation should be made after determining what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO) it is non-statutory and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 for such a rejection (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)(1)). If the claim fails Step 1 but applicant’s disclosure suggests the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, proceed to analyze whether an amended claim would qualify under Pathway A, B or C and recommend an amendment if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine invention and apply Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before performing the eligibility steps, an examiner should determine what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2111 for information on BRI. It is a best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment if the BRI encompasses non-statutory embodiments so that the claim may be narrowed to statutory embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims fail Step 1 (Step 1: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Examiner should point out the BRI and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to those embodiments that fall within a statutory category. Example: machine-readable media whose BRI encompasses non-statutory transitory signals (e.g., carrier waves) should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2A: Whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A is the first part of the Alice/Mayo test and asks whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon (product of nature), or an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim as a whole is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO), it is eligible at Pathway B and the eligibility analysis concludes. If the claim as a whole is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), further analysis under Step 2B is required to determine if the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A is a two-prong inquiry (Prong One and Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A consists of Prong One: determine whether the claim recites (sets forth or describes) an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon; and Prong Two: determine whether the recited judicial exception is integrated into a practical application by additional claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both prongs together answer whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception. If Prong One is negative (no recitation), the claim is eligible at Pathway B. If Prong One is affirmative, analyze Prong Two to see if the claim integrates the exception into a practical application (if so, Step 2A: NO; if not, Step 2A: YES and proceed to Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prong One: Does the claim recite a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong One asks whether a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea is set forth or described in the claim. 'Set forth' and 'described' indicate two ways an exception can be recited in a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should (1) identify the specific claim limitation(s) they believe recite an exception and (2) determine whether those limitations fall within at least one judicial-exception grouping. Distinguish claims that 'recite' an exception from those that merely 'involve' one (example: Diehr/Mayo claims that explicitly state a formula versus Alice-style claims that describe a concept). Example: a claim reciting 'elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' sets forth a law of nature and thus recites an exception, while a teeter-totter claim that is based on the principle of a lever merely involves an exception and does not recite it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prong Two: Do additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application?
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two asks whether the claim's additional elements integrate the recited judicial exception into a practical application. If they do, the claim is not directed to the exception (Step 2A: NO); if they do not, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires Step 2B analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere inclusion of a judicial exception (e.g., a mathematical formula) means the claim 'recites' an exception under Prong One, but does not automatically mean the claim is 'directed to' that exception. The additional elements must 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception (Alice). If there are no additional elements or if the additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient to integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional elements must transform the claim; adding another exception is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible, additional claim elements must transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception; merely adding elements that are themselves judicial exceptions (or adding one abstract idea to another) is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as RecogniCorp (adding one abstract idea to another) and Genetic Technologies (eligibility cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature itself) illustrate that stacking exceptions or having only the exception(s) present will not satisfy eligibility. If no sufficient additional elements exist, recommend amendment where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling claims reciting multiple judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may recite multiple judicial exceptions (e.g., two abstract ideas, or an abstract idea plus a law of nature). Examiners should apply the same eligibility analysis regardless of the number of exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless clearly distinct, care should be taken not to parse the claim into multiple exceptions—consider treating limitations together as a single abstract idea for Prong Two and Step 2B. If exceptions are distinct (e.g., one limitation describes a law of nature and another recites an abstract idea), the examiner may select one exception for efficiency; if integrating that selected exception into a practical application or showing 'significantly more' is successful, the claim should be considered eligible. If neither selected nor other exceptions are integrated or shown to be 'significantly more,' the claim is ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated groupings of abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: To facilitate examination, abstract ideas are organized into three enumerated groupings: (1) Mathematical concepts — mathematical relationships, formulas, calculations; (2) Certain methods of organizing human activity — fundamental economic principles or practices, commercial/legal interactions, managing personal behavior or relationships; (3) Mental processes — concepts performed in the human mind (observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify the specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an abstract idea and determine whether those limitations fall within at least one of these groupings. If they do, proceed to Prong Two; if they do not, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the abstract-idea exception analysis concludes (except in rare circumstances). See MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) for detailed discussion and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern and its role in eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying concern motivating the judicial exceptions is preemption — that monopolization of basic tools (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) could impede innovation. However, preemption is not a standalone test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions of preemption are inherent in and resolved by the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B). The absence of complete preemption does not demonstrate eligibility; likewise, a preemptive claim may be ineligible. Examiners should therefore apply the Alice/Mayo test rather than rely on preemption alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practice: recommend amendments to resolve eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim fails Step 1 or when it appears a claim could be amended to resolve eligibility issues, the examiner should recommend an amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, suggest claim amendments that narrow scope to statutory embodiments or add elements that integrate a judicial exception into a practical application. When making a Step 1 rejection, use the appropriate form paragraphs and advise applicant of the BRI and possible amendments (see MPEP § 2106.07 and related guidance).
